Data Processing Models and Real-Time Systems

14 sources·Oct 14, 2026

The provided sources explore the core principles of real-time programming, focusing on how systems must maintain both logical and temporal correctness. They detail various data processing models—such as batch, interactive, and real-time—and emphasize that real-time systems are defined by predictability and worst-case response times rather than raw speed. Additionally, the materials examine embedded systems, illustrating their anatomy and widespread use across critical industries like automotive and aerospace. Finally, the texts cover dependability attributes, failure classifications, and the fault-error-failure chain, highlighting methods for achieving system reliability and fault tolerance.

Sunday, October 18

Classify each failure mode and say whether it is in the value or time domain: (a) a temperature sensor reports −500 °C; (b) a brake command arrives 20 ms after its deadline; (c) a heartbeat message is never sent.

(a) Value domain — Constraint error: The reported value (−500 °C) falls outside the physically valid range. (b) Time domain — Performance error (too late): The brake command is delivered 20 ms after its specified deadline. (c) Time domain — Omission error (infinitely late): The heartbeat message is never delivered.
💡 Would you like to move on to question 33 to review NMR module counts and Byzantine fault tolerance?

(a) How many modules does NMR need to mask 2 faults? (b) How many components are needed to tolerate 2 Byzantine faults? (c) Why is the voter a single point of failure, and how can this be removed?

(a) 5 modules (formula: N=2m+1=2(2)+1=5)
(b) 7 components (formula: N=3f+1=3(2)+1=7)
(c)
  • Why it is a single point of failure: The voter is in series with the entire system; if the single voter fails, the system fails regardless of module health.
  • How it can be removed: Triplicate the voters so each downstream component receives input from its own dedicated voter (or use distributed voting).

Give three reasons why fault prevention alone is never enough for a critical real-time system.

  1. Exhaustive testing is mathematically impossible: The input, execution state, and timing interleaving space of complex real-time software is too vast to test all possible combinations.
  2. Specification and environment mismatches: Requirements or specification flaws often remain undetected until deployment, as realistic operational conditions (e.g., severe crash impacts or missile interceptions) are hard or impossible to fully replicate during testing.
  3. Hardware wear-out and random physical faults: Even if software could be rendered entirely defect-free, underlying hardware components inevitably degrade, wear out, or experience random environmental interference (such as cosmic-ray bit flips) during operation.
💡 Would you like to move on to question 35 to review exact, median, and tolerance voting across temperature sensors?

Three correct temperature sensors read 50.2 °C, 50.4 °C and 58.9 °C. (a) Why would an exact voter fail? (b) What value does median (mid-value select) voting output? (c) Using tolerance voting with ε = 0.5 and averaging the agreeing values, what is the output? (3)

(a) Why an exact voter fails: An exact voter requires bit-for-bit or identical numerical equality among inputs to form a majority. Analog sensor readings naturally contain continuous variations and noise, so all three values are distinct (50.2 ≠ 50.4 ≠ 58.9), causing the exact voter to find no majority and report an error.
(b) Median (mid-value select) output: 50.4 °C (Sorting the readings gives 50.2 °C, 50.4 °C, 58.9 °C; the middle value is 50.4 °C).
(c) Tolerance voting output: 50.3 °C (50.2 °C and 50.4 °C agree within ε = 0.5 since |50.2 − 50.4| = 0.2 ≤ 0.5, whereas 58.9 °C is an outlier; averaging the two agreeing values gives (50.2 + 50.4) / 2 = 50.3 °C).
💡 Would you like to move on to question 36 to classify the tasks in the SkyLine driverless metro scenario as hard, firm, or soft real-time?

Section B — Scenario (Q36–Q40: 5 × 3 = 15 marks) Read the story, then answer Q36–Q40. The SkyLine driverless metro SkyLine is a fictional driverless metro train. Each train has an onboard computer that runs several functions: an emergency braking task that must apply the brakes within 50 ms of an obstacle being detected; a passenger information display that shows the next station; and a CCTV stream that sends 30 frames per second to the control room, where a frame that arrives late is simply dropped. Train speed is measured by three identical speed sensors (each R = 0.9) feeding a majority voter. To save cost, sensors 2 and 3 were wired to the same power supply. One evening that supply failed, both sensors read 0 km/h, and the voter outvoted the correct sensor 1. The train thought it was stopped and did not slow down for a curve; luckily the driver-assist system in the control room noticed and stopped it remotely. Investigators also found a second problem. A programmer had written the speed-limit check using m/s instead of km/h. During a test run, the stored speed limit became 3.6 times too high, and the train entered a station faster than allowed. The braking controller runs as a hot-standby pair with heartbeats every 50 ms. Last month the primary controller threw an unexpected exception halfway through a braking command; the brakes had already been partly applied. Engineers debated whether to roll the controller back to its last checkpoint and retry, or to move it straight to a safe state. Each braking controller has MTTF = 4000 h. Today a broken controller is fixed by a technician from the depot, with MTTR = 8 h. Management is considering keeping a spare controller on every platform, which would cut MTTR to 2 h.

  1. Classify the emergency braking task, the passenger information display and the CCTV stream as hard, firm or soft real-time. Justify each in one line. (3)
  2. (a) Calculate the reliability of the speed-sensor TMR system assuming a perfect voter and independent failures. (b) Name the type of failure that happened when the power supply failed, and suggest one way to prevent it. (3)
  3. For the m/s versus km/h problem, identify the fault, the error and the failure. (3)
  4. Is the SkyLine train a fail-safe or fail-operational system? For the controller exception, should engineers use backward recovery (roll back and retry) or forward recovery (safe state)? Justify your answer. (3)
  5. Calculate the availability and yearly downtime (8760 h) of one braking controller with MTTR = 8 h, and again with MTTR = 2 h. Which dependability parameter does the platform spare improve? (3)
Question 36
  • Emergency braking task: Hard real-time — Missing the 50 ms deadline can result in a collision, causing catastrophic damage or loss of human life.
  • Passenger information display: Soft real-time — Missing a deadline (e.g., late station update) merely degrades user experience, but the late information still retains some value.
  • CCTV stream: Firm real-time — Late frames have zero value and are discarded, but occasionally dropping a frame causes no catastrophic damage.
Question 37
  • (a) TMR System Reliability: 0.972 (or 97.2%) RTMR​=3R2−2R3=3(0.9)2−2(0.9)3=2.43−1.458=0.972
  • (b) Failure Type & Prevention:
    • Failure Type: Common-mode failure — A single shared power supply failure caused multiple redundant sensors (sensors 2 and 3) to fail simultaneously.
    • Prevention: Hardware separation / power independence — Wire each sensor to a separate, independent power supply to eliminate the single point of failure.
Question 38
  • Fault: Software design/coding defect — The programmer implemented the speed-limit check using m/s instead of km/h.
  • Error: Incorrect internal state — The stored speed-limit variable in memory became 3.6 times too high.
  • Failure: Observable system deviation — The train entered the station at a speed higher than permitted.
Question 39
  • System Type: Fail-safe system — A known safe state exists (applying emergency brakes to bring the train to a complete stop).
  • Recovery Choice: Forward recovery (safe state) — The exception occurred while the brakes were already partly applied; rolling back state and retrying introduces unpredictable timing delays during a critical braking sequence, whereas forward recovery immediately transitions the train to a safe state (full emergency braking).
Question 40
(MTTF = 4000 h)
  • With MTTR = 8 h:
    • Availability: A=MTTF+MTTRMTTF​=40084000​≈0.9980(99.80%)
    • Yearly Downtime: (1−A)×8760 h=(40088​)×8760≈17.48 hours/year
  • With MTTR = 2 h:
    • Availability: A=40024000​≈0.9995(99.95%)
    • Yearly Downtime: (1−A)×8760 h=(40022​)×8760≈4.38 hours/year
  • Dependability Parameter Improved: Maintainability (which directly increases Availability).

a) Calculate the reliability of the speed-sensor TMR system assuming a perfect voter and independent failures. (b) Name the type of failure that happened when the power supply failed, and suggest one way to prevent it.

(a) Reliability of the speed-sensor TMR system: 0.972 (or 97.2%). RTMR​=3R2−2R3=3(0.9)2−2(0.9)3=2.43−1.458=0.972
(b) Failure Type & Prevention:
  • Failure Type: Common-mode failure — A single shared power supply failure caused both redundant sensors (sensors 2 and 3) to fail simultaneously, overriding the majority voter.
  • Prevention: Power independence / hardware separation — Wire each sensor to its own separate, independent power supply to eliminate the single point of failure.

For the m/s versus km/h problem, identify the fault, the error and the failure.

  • Fault: Software design/coding defect — the programmer wrote the speed-limit check using m/s instead of km/h.
  • Error: Incorrect internal system state — the stored speed-limit variable in memory became 3.6 times too high.
  • Failure: Observable system deviation — the train entered the station at a speed higher than permitted.

Is the SkyLine train a fail-safe or fail-operational system? For the controller exception, should engineers use backward recovery (roll back and retry) or forward recovery (safe state)? Justify your answer.

  • System classification: Fail-safe system
    • Justification: A known safe state exists—applying the emergency brakes to bring the train to a complete stop.
  • Recovery method: Forward recovery (moving straight to a safe state)
    • Justification: The primary controller threw an exception halfway through a braking command, leaving the brakes partly applied. Performing backward recovery (rolling back to a checkpoint and retrying) introduces unpredictable timing delays during a time-critical braking operation. Forward recovery bypasses retries and immediately forces the train into a safe state (applying full emergency braking).

Calculate the availability and yearly downtime (8760 h) of one braking controller with MTTR = 8 h, and again with MTTR = 2 h. Which dependability parameter does the platform spare improve?

With MTTR = 8 hours
  • Availability: 0.9980 (or 99.80%) A=MTTF+MTTRMTTF​=4000+84000​=40084000​≈0.9980
  • Yearly Downtime: 17.48 hours/year (or ~17.5 h) Downtime=(1−A)×8760 h=(40088​)×8760≈17.48 hours
With MTTR = 2 hours (Platform Spare)
  • Availability: 0.9995 (or 99.95%) A=4000+24000​=40024000​≈0.9995
  • Yearly Downtime: 4.38 hours/year Downtime=(1−A)×8760 h=(40022​)×8760≈4.38 hours
Dependability Parameter Improved
  • Maintainability: Keeping a spare controller directly reduces repair time (MTTR), which improves maintainability and consequently boosts system availability.
